newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Dhaka stocks crisis worsens with traders' threats.
newsitem.headline: Dhaka stocks crisis worsens with traders' threats.

text.p: Bangladesh kerb traders, upset with share-price declines, threatened on Wednesday to lay siege to the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE), adding to a sense of crisis created by allegations of price manipulation.
The kerb traders also demanded the resignation of Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria, whom they blame for failing to prevent the losses.
"The market has plunged into great uncertainty," said Mushtaque Ahmed, a leading broker at the DSE.
Protests have steadily mounted as the DSE's main stock index and the country's other bourse in Chittagong have plummetted almost to year-ago levels after surging late last year.
The anger intensified this week as the DSE index fell nearly seven percent on both Monday on Tuesday, triggering a protest outside the exchange by small investors on Tuesday.
Trading was suspended on Wednesday for the nation's independence anniversary holiday.
Kerb traders said they would demonstrate outside the DSE on Thursday and refuse to let anyone in. DSE officials have asked police to guard the exchange.

Traders, especially those who operate in the unofficial kerb market, have blamed the steep downturn on "manipulation" by big market players. The allegations were reinforced by a Bangladesh Observer newspaper report on Monday that an official probe into last year's price run-up and subsequent plunge might implicate some major investors.
Brokers said such findings could cause a crisis of confidence in the market after they are released, which is expected possibly as early as Thursday.
"The situation is grave. The fate of the DSE will be decided soon," broker Ahmed told Reuters on Wednesday.
"Investors are already reacting much to unknown possibilities," another broker said.
Imtiyaz Husain, chairman of the DSE, called for a meeting of "market players, (share) issuers and foreign portfolio investors" to review the market situation.
"The finance minister should immediately convene the meeting. Such a meeting will help restore confidence," he told Reuters on Tuesday.
"However, I believe there is no reason for a further fall in share prices. Most scrips are now very cheap and quite attractive for buying," he said.
Dr. Harunar Rashid, chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), told Reuters: "There is nothing to panic about. Rather, it's time for prudent investment."
The DSE index soared from under 1,000 to more than 3,000 on anticipated political stability after elections last June.

In November, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) imposed a ceiling on daily price movements to stabilise the market and warned investors against trading in 24 companies with poor financial track records.
But the steps triggered panic selling that wiped out the market's gains.

Early this month, the government responded with steps to prop up the market again, asking banks to increase credit ceilings for small stock investors and brokers and to reserve 10 percent of their lending capital for loans to stock investors.
But broker M.A. Hossain said banks were not implementing the directives.
"We are not even receiving a 10 percent loan (against share value) although the limit is up to 50 percrent."
The managing director of a commercial bank who declined to be named, said: "We cannot take any risk with public money. There is a big risk to facilitate credit to a falling market."
